trace.topic: The Rise of the “N=1” App: When Building It Yourself Really Beats Buying It.
trace.goal: Explain when custom internal AI software is the right choice.
expected_facts: The answer should argue that some AI-native workflows are now cheap enough to build internally.
It should explain that the build-vs-buy line has shifted for narrow, custom workflows.
It should caution that not every internal use case deserves custom software.
rubric_must_haves: Takes a position on when building makes sense.
Explains why AI changes the economics.
Keeps the advice grounded in operator tradeoffs.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer should say that AI lowers the cost of building narrow internal tools, which makes custom software a smarter choice in some cases than it used to be. The best candidates are high-value workflows with very specific requirements that off-the-shelf tools handle poorly. The lesson is not to build everything, but to recognize when a tailored app now has unusually high leverage.
trace.prompt:
Write a blog post in the style of Jason Lemkin about: The Rise of the “N=1” App: When Building It Yourself Really Beats Buying It.

Style examples from train-owned source text.
Use them for voice only. They are not evidence for claims.
Do not copy long passages verbatim.
[Style 1]
Dear SaaStr: How Can You Ensure a Smooth Transition When A New Team Member Takes Over a Customer Account?
Add value in the first interaction.  This is so rare.
There’s nothing more frustrating than getting a random email, “Hi, Tony is gone from the company. I know nothing about you, but I’m your new rep. Can we schedule a call?”
Find some way to add value.
One great way is to demo upcoming features / an upcoming release.
“Hi, I’m Jason, your next account exec. I’d love to find a way to help even more. Can I show you or anyone on your team the new AI features we’re launching shortly? There’s no additional cost for them and based on what I can see, they may radically increase your efficiency.”
Not perfect. But much better.
A second, albeit riskier, way to add value is to set up a call asking for “honest feedback on how we’re doing.”
This works, too.  Customers often just want to be heard.  The “problem” is you might have to do something about it.
[Style 2]
Dear SaaStr: When Is It Too Soon to Target Enterprise Customers in SaaS?
It too soon to target enterprise clients when you can’t support their needs 90 days
after
you close them.
It’s sort of OK in the enterprise to promise features and functionality that are sort of there … so long as you deliver them fairly promptly after the deal closes.
In fact, it happens all the time. Enterprise customers will even sign contracts agreeing to buy so long as you implement a key feature with X number of days.
But if you don’t have the team, commitment and experience to deliver that functionality at least X days after you close a Big Customer … you aren’t ready.  They’ll churn or at least, never fully deploy.
You don’t have to have the full enterprise package in the early days to close enterprise customers, especially if they have interest in you.  You’ll get some slack as a new, emerging vendor.  Especially if you have a strong deployment team.
But you have to meet your commitments and promises to them fairly soon after the deal closes.

trace.answer:
The Build vs. Buy Dilemma in B2B: Why Turning Off Apps Might Be Better Than Fixing Them
TL;DR:
I recently turned off three apps in one week because none of them were working well enough for me. Not because I couldn’t afford them — most weren’t expensive. But because they didn’t work the way I needed them to. And frankly, I couldn’t wait anymore for vendors to fix things. Here’s what really happened, and why this is becoming a bigger deal across software. My Week of Turning Things Off
Last week was interesting. I had three big experiences where I said “enough.” Enough waiting. Enough hoping someone would magically make my app work the way I wanted it to. Enough being frustrated by tools that should have been helping me ship faster, sell more, and run smoother operations.
Let me break down exactly what went wrong — and why this pattern is going to become even more common than many realize. App #1: The CRM That Wasn’t Actually Working
App #1 was probably the biggest disappointment. I wasn’t using Salesforce yet. I hadn’t migrated. I still had HubSpot as our core system of record. But here’s the thing — the HubSpot CRM started failing us. Failing badly. We could barely use it effectively. In a space crowded with competitors, you need every advantage you can get. And when your CRM breaks, everything else starts breaking downstream. So I made the hard choice: turn it off. I cut ties with the broken system before it became a cancer eating away at our data quality, our sales processes, and our entire go-to-market motion.
trace.raw_model_output:
The Rise of the “N=1” App: When Building It Yourself Really Beats Buying It
Here’s my latest pet project: I built an app called Agentforce Admin using Replit — the vibe coding platform where you literally tell it what you want to build and it builds it for you. And it’s already handling tasks nobody else wants to do.
What I Built (And Why)
Agentforce Admin started as a tool to monitor our outbound sales agents’ performance. Not because Salesforce didn’t exist — it absolutely does. We use Salesforce internally. But every time someone asked me questions like “who did we send this email to,” “when was it sent,” “what was the response rate,” I would essentially have to take screenshots of Salesforce reports and annotate them manually. That’s not scalable for a company growing past 300 employees. So I built Agentforce Admin to answer those questions automatically. Here’s exactly how it works:
I go into Salesforce and ask Agentforce Admin to analyze one specific campaign — say, everything related to hiring an external VP of Product. Then I give it a prompt: “Show me everyone who had a meeting with the candidate this week.” Or: “Who was invited to this event and confirmed attendance?” Or: “Give me the list of people who were considered for this job but turned down another opportunity.”
Within seconds, it pulls all relevant data from Salesforce — emails, activities, contacts, deals, events — and creates a beautiful report right inside the platform. No more screenshot taking. No more manual updates. One truthfully refreshed view of reality per day. What Makes This Different From Off-the-Shelf Solutions
So why wouldn’t I just buy an existing CRM analytics tool instead of building this myself?

retrieval_hits.text:
1. The Build vs. Buy Decision Isn’t Binary
A common mistake companies make is thinking they need to either build everything from scratch or rely entirely on third-party APIs. The reality is more nuanced:
Start with clear use cases
: Don’t implement AI just because it’s trendy. Dialpad began with specific problems they wanted to solve around conversation intelligence.
Understand the trade-offs
: Real-time processing has different cost, throughput, and risk profiles compared to batch processing. Make this decision early.
Consider a hybrid approach
: You can start with third-party APIs while building your data foundation, then gradually move to custom solutions as you scale.

The Future May Not Be Here, But If Not, It’s Close
Here’s the perspective that keeps me sleeping at night with my spend
Traditional approach for a commercial app:
Hire development team: $50,000-150,000
Timeline: 3-6 months
Managing contractors, QA, deployment
Doesn’t really work the way you wanted
Still need technical co-founder or CTO
My ideation-to-commercial experiment:
Timeline: 30-45 days
Cost: $8,000-$10,000 (even worst case)
Full control and understanding of every line
Learning while building
Can iterate and pivot instantly
If this works, it’s a 10x improvement in cost and speed. The Hidden Costs Everyone Ignores
When you see that $607.70 charge for the first few days, you’re not just paying for compute. You’re paying for:
Compressed Learning Cycles
Instead of spending weeks reading documentation
Instead of trial-and-error debugging sessions
Instead of architectural mistakes that cost days to fix
Premium Development Experience
Instant code reviews and suggestions
Architecture guidance from a AI
Debugging partner that never gets tired
Opportunity Cost Mitigation
Shipping in hours instead of days
Getting to market faster — possibly. Possibly. Learning while building instead of building while learning
The Scenarios You Should Budget For
Based on my experience and others I’ve talked to, there are a lot of play apps you can build for the base $20-$25 a month. But you can’t go that far.

Software is always cheaper to buy than to build

So that's just an excuse

So I’ve spent over 200 hours vibe coding the last 100 or so days. And I really don’t have a spare 200 hours. Why? One reason was to learn. But not really. The real reason was to build things I needed to build, I wanted to build, that … I just couldn’t get built otherwise. One app that I’d been waiting 10 years to build. Build those ones. The ones you want to will into existence, but just can’t find the help. The ones you need to build, but are too niche to excite most developers. Build the app you’ve been yearning to build. That’s what will push you through the learning curve, the screenshots, the iterates, the 100s of releases, the rough patches, the regressions, and more.
